excerpts: MCP Support / Open WebUI This documentation explains how to easily set up and deploy the MCP (Model Context Protocol)-to-OpenAPI proxy server (mcpo) provided by Open WebUI.
Learn how you can expose MCP-based tool servers using standard, familiar OpenAPI endpoints suitable for end-users and developers.

This documentation explains how to easily set up and deploy the [**MCP (Model Context Protocol)-to-OpenAPI proxy server** (mcpo)](https://github.com/open-webui/mcpo) provided by Open WebUI. Learn how you can expose MCP-based tool servers using standard, familiar OpenAPI endpoints suitable for end-users and developers.
This page covers `mcpo` , the MCP-to-OpenAPI bridge.

The MCP-to-OpenAPI proxy server lets you use tool servers implemented with MCP (Model Context Protocol) directly via standard REST/OpenAPI APIs, with no need to manage unfamiliar or complicated custom protocols. If you're an end-user or application developer, this means you can interact easily with powerful MCP-based tooling directly through familiar REST-like endpoints.

While MCP tool servers are powerful and flexible, they commonly communicate via standard input/output (stdio), often running on your local machine where they can easily access your filesystem, environment, and other native system capabilities. That’s a strength, but also a limitation. If you want to deploy your main interface (like Open WebUI) on the cloud, you quickly run into a problem: your cloud instance can’t speak directly to an MCP server running locally on your machine via stdio.

MCP servers typically rely on raw stdio communication, which is: 🔓 Inherently insecure across environments ❌ Incompatible with most modern tools, UIs, or platforms 🧩 Lacking critical features like authentication, documentation, and error handling

The mcpo proxy addresses those issues: ✅ Instantly compatible with existing OpenAPI tools, SDKs, and clients 🛡 Wraps your tools with secure, scalable, and standards-based HTTP endpoints 🧠 Auto-generates interactive OpenAPI documentation for every tool, entirely config-free 🔌 Uses plain HTTP, with no socket setup, daemon juggling, or platform-specific glue code

**Prerequisites** **Python 3.8+** with `pip` installed. MCP-compatible application (for example: `mcp-server-time` ) (Optional but recommended) `uv` installed for faster startup and zero-config convenience.
**Install mcpo** Using **uv** (recommended): ``` uvx mcpo --port 8000 -- your_mcp_server_command ```

🔑 **Translating this MCP setup to a quick local proxy command** : You can easily run the recommended MCP server ( `mcp-server-time` ) directly through the **MCP-to-OpenAPI proxy** ( `mcpo` ) like this: ``` uvx mcpo --port 8000 -- uvx mcp-server-time --local-timezone=America/New_York ``` That's it! You're now running the MCP-to-OpenAPI Proxy locally and exposing the powerful **MCP Time Server** through standard OpenAPI endpoints accessible at: 📖 **Interactive OpenAPI Documentation:** [`http://localhost:8000/docs`](http://localhost:8000/docs) Feel free to replace `uvx mcp-server-time --local-timezone=America/New_York` with your preferred MCP Server command from other available MCP implementations found in the official repository.

🚀 Accessing the Generated APIs ​ As soon as it starts, the MCP Proxy ( `mcpo` ) automatically: Discovers MCP tools dynamically and generates REST endpoints. Creates interactive, human-readable OpenAPI documentation accessible at: `http://localhost:8000/docs` Simply call the auto-generated API endpoints directly via HTTP clients, AI agents, or other OpenAPI tools of your preference.

**Dynamic Schema Discovery & Endpoints:** At server startup, the proxy connects to the MCP server to query available tools. It automatically builds FastAPI endpoints based on the MCP tool schemas, creating concise and clear REST endpoints. **OpenAPI Auto-documentation:** Endpoints generated are seamlessly documented and available via FastAPI's built-in Swagger UI ( `/docs` ). No extra doc writing required.

If you want to use the published mcpo image instead of building your own image, bind the proxy to `0.0.0.0` so Docker port publishing can reach it: ``` docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/open-webui/mcpo:main \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ --api-key "top-secret" \ -- your_mcp_server_command ```

Critical for Persistence If you connect Open WebUI to this proxy using an API Key or Auth Token, you **MUST** set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` in your Open WebUI Docker config. If this key changes (e.g., on container restart), Open WebUI will fail to decrypt the stored credentials for your tool.

Uses RAG to find and inject the most relevant chunks based on the user's query. When hybrid search is enabled ( `ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH` ), retrieval combines BM25 keyword search with vector search, plus reranking for accuracy.

File processing happens asynchronously. You must poll the status endpoint until processing completes before adding files to a knowledge base, or you'll get an "empty content" error. See API Endpoints for workflow examples.

Processing delay for API uploads ​ Files uploaded via API are processed asynchronously. Attempting to use a file before processing completes will fail silently or return empty results. Note that uploading with a `knowledge_id` (above) makes linking server-side and robust to client disconnects, but it does **not** make the content instantly queryable: extraction/embedding still runs in the background, so poll `GET /api/v1/files/{id}/process/status` before relying on retrieval.

Knowledge is NOT auto-injected with native function calling When native function calling is enabled, attached knowledge is **not automatically injected** . The model must call the knowledge tools to search and retrieve. If your model isn't using attached knowledge: **Add system prompt instructions** telling the model to use `list_knowledge` and `query_knowledge_files` . **Disable native function calling** for that model to restore automatic RAG injection.

Agentic Knowledge Tools ​ With native function calling enabled, models interact with your knowledge bases using built-in tools. ... The two search tools complement each other: | |`query_knowledge_files` |`grep_knowledge_files` | |**How it matches** |Semantic / vector retrieval (with optional BM25 + rerank when `ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH` is on) |Exact string match, regex auto-detected (e.g. `error|warn` , `version \d+` ) | |**Returns** |Relevant chunks of content |Matching lines with file ID, filename, and 1-indexed line number | |**Use when** |"What does the documentation say about X?" for paraphrased questions, conceptual lookups |"Find every place we mention `OPENAI_API_KEY` " for literal identifiers, error strings, version numbers | |**Result cap** |Top K (default 5) |50 matches ( `KNOWLEDGE_GREP_MAX_MATCHES` ) | |**Flags** |(none) |`case_insensitive` , `count_only` , `file_id` (single-file mode) | In agentic flows, a typical pattern is: `query_knowledge_files` to locate the relevant document, then `grep_knowledge_files` to pinpoint exact lines, then `view_file` (line-range mode below) to read the surrounding context.

Filesystem-style access ( `kb_exec` ) ​ When `ENABLE_KB_EXEC=True` is set, Open WebUI exposes a `kb_exec` tool that gives the model a filesystem-style interface over knowledge bases. **Tools that go away** , because their function is now covered by `kb_exec` commands: `list_knowledge` : replaced by `ls` `search_knowledge_files` : replaced by `find "<glob>"` `grep_knowledge_files` : replaced by `grep "<pattern>"` `view_file` and `view_knowledge_file` : replaced by `cat` , `head` , `tail` , `sed -n '<a>,<b>p'` **Tools that stay injected alongside `kb_exec`** , because they do something `kb_exec` can't: **`query_knowledge_files`** : semantic / RAG search (always) **`view_note`** : when notes are attached to the model ( `kb_exec` is file-only, so notes need a dedicated reader) **`query_knowledge_bases`** and **`search_knowledge_bases`** : when no KB is attached to the model, so the model can still discover and search across knowledge bases by name/description It is **off by default** and still experimental, but for an enhanced agentic RAG experience we recommend enabling it ( `ENABLE_KB_EXEC=True` ) for capable models running native function calling. It targets frontier models that already "think in shell": they tend to chain `ls` , `grep` and `cat` more reliably than they orchestrate a fan-out of specialized tools. It only works with native function calling on; for models set to Legacy it has no effect.

🔍 Focused Retrieval (default) ​") Uses RAG to find and inject the most relevant chunks based on the user's query. When hybrid search is enabled ( `ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH` ), retrieval combines BM25 keyword search with vector search, plus reranking for accuracy. Best for large document sets where only specific sections are relevant. 📄 Full Context ​ Injects the complete content of the file into every message. No chunking, no semantic search. Always injected regardless of native function calling settings, so the model doesn't need to call any tools to access it. Best for short reference documents, style guides, or context that's always relevant.

Knowledge is where you store the files and collections that your AI can search, read, and reason over. Upload PDFs, spreadsheets, code, or any text-based document. Build collections around projects, teams, or topics. When a model needs an answer, it pulls from your knowledge base instead of guessing. Unlike Notes , which inject full content into every message, Knowledge uses retrieval (RAG) to find the relevant chunks on demand. This makes it the right choice for large document sets where injecting everything would exceed the context window.

Agentic Knowledge Tools ​ With native function calling enabled, models interact with your knowledge bases using built-in tools. Which tools appear depends on whether specific knowledge is attached to the model: Files inside a knowledge base, with search and sort |Tool |Attached KB |No KB attached |Description | |`list_knowledge` |✅ |❌ |List attached KBs (with file counts), standalone files, and notes; pass `knowledge_id` (with `skip` / `count` , max 200) to page one KB's files | |`list_knowledge_bases` |❌ |✅ |Browse available knowledge bases with file counts | |`search_knowledge_bases` |❌ |✅ |Find knowledge bases by name or description | |`query_knowledge_bases` |❌ |✅ |Search KB names/descriptions by semantic similarity | |`search_knowledge_files` |✅ (scoped) |✅ (all) |Search files by filename | |`query_knowledge_files` |✅ (scoped) |✅ |Search file contents using the RAG pipeline | |`grep_knowledge_files` |✅ (scoped) |✅ |Exact text / regex search across knowledge files (returns matching lines with line numbers; auto-detects regex like `error | |`view_file` |✅ |❌ |Read file content with pagination ( `offset` / `max_chars` ) or by line range ( `start_line` / `end_line` , optional `line_numbers` ) | |`view_knowledge_file` |✅ |✅ |Read file content from any accessible KB | |`view_note` |✅ |❌ |Read attached notes | "Attached" here covers knowledge on the model, knowledge on the chat's folder, and knowledge bases or notes attached to the chat itself when the model's **File Context** capability is off. Whatever the source, the model is told what it has: its system prompt carries an `<attached_knowledge>` list of the items with their IDs, so it can point a query at one knowledge base rather than searching blind. The key split: `list_knowledge` and `list_knowledge_bases` are mutually exclusive. Attaching a KB scopes the model to only those documents. Leaving it unscoped lets the model discover everything the user has access to. When to prefer `grep_knowledge_files` over `query_knowledge_files` ​ The two search tools complement each other: | |`query_knowledge_files` |`grep_knowledge_files` | |**How it matches** |Semantic / vector retrieval (with optional BM25 + rerank when `ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH` is on) |Exact string match, regex auto-detected (e.g. `error|warn` , `version \d+` ) | |**Returns** |Relevant chunks of content |Matching lines with file ID, filename, and 1-indexed line number | |**Use when** |"What does the documentation say about X?" for paraphrased questions, conceptual lookups |"Find every place we mention `OPENAI_API_KEY` " for literal identifiers, error strings, version numbers | |**Result cap** |Top K (default 5) |50 matches ( `KNOWLEDGE_GREP_MAX_MATCHES` ) | |**Flags** |(none) |`case_insensitive` , `count_only` , `file_id` (single-file mode) | In agentic flows, a typical pattern is: `query_knowledge_files` to locate the relevant document, then `grep_knowledge_files` to pinpoint exact lines, then `view_file` (line-range mode below) to read the surrounding context.

excerpts: Functions / Open WebUI Functions are modular Python plugins that extend the capabilities of Open WebUI itself. While Tools give LLMs the ability to call external APIs during inference, Functions change how the platform behaves at a deeper level.
Functions are **modular Python plugins** that extend the capabilities of Open WebUI itself.
Functions are stored in the database as Python source code, dynamically loaded at runtime, and executed server-side.
Administrators create and manage them; regular users interact with the results.
Open WebUI supports four types of Functions. The type is **auto-detected** from the class name in your Python code, so you never need to configure it manually.

|**Pipe** |`class Pipe` |Adds a custom model or agent |Appears as a selectable model in the chat sidebar | |**Filter** |`class Filter` |Intercepts data flowing to/from models |Runs transparently as middleware on existing models | |**Action** |`class Action` |Adds interactive buttons to messages |Appears as a clickable button on chat messages | |**Event** |`class Event` |Runs custom logic in response to system events |Runs in the background; no direct UI |

When you save a Function, Open WebUI scans the Python source code for a top-level class named `Pipe` , `Filter` , `Action` , or `Event` . The first match determines the function type. You never need to manually set the type because it's inferred from the code.
While Tools give LLMs the ability to call external APIs during inference, Functions change how the platform behaves at a deeper level.

|Give the LLM access to live data (weather, stocks, APIs) |**Tool** |Tools are called by the model during inference | |Add a model provider with a non-OpenAI API |**Pipe Function** |Pipes register as models in the sidebar | |Build a non-LLM interface (search, databases, smart home) |**Pipe Function** |Pipes handle the entire request without needing an LLM | |Build a multi-step agent with custom logic |**Pipe Function** |Pipes control the full request/response cycle |

Go to **Admin Panel → Functions** . Click **Import from URL** and paste a link to the Python file. GitHub URLs are automatically converted to raw file URLs. Review and save. Create Manually ​ Go to **Admin Panel → Functions** . Click **Create** . Enter an ID (alphanumeric and underscores only), name, and description. Write your Python code in the editor. Click **Save** . The function type is auto-detected from your code.
Functions are managed from **Admin Panel → Functions** .

A triple-quoted docstring at the top of the file is parsed as YAML frontmatter for metadata: ``` """ title: My Custom Function author: your_name author_url: https://github.com/your_name version: 1.0.0 icon_url: https://example.com/icon.svg required_open_webui_version: 0.4.0 requirements: requests, beautifulsoup4 """ ``` |Field |Purpose | |`title` |Display name in the admin UI | |`author` / `author_url` |Attribution metadata | |`version` |Version identifier | |`icon_url` |Icon displayed next to the function name (use a URL, not base64) | |`required_open_webui_version` |Minimum compatible Open WebUI version | |`requirements` |Comma-separated list of pip packages to auto-install | Automatic Dependency Installation When `requirements` is specified in the frontmatter, Open WebUI automatically installs the listed packages via `pip` the first time the function loads.

Automatic Dependency Installation When `requirements` is specified in the frontmatter, Open WebUI automatically installs the listed packages via `pip` the first time the function loads. This is controlled by the `PIP_INSTALL_FRONTMATTER_REQUIREMENTS` environment variable (enabled by default).

**Functions execute arbitrary Python code on your server.** Function creation is restricted to administrators only. Only install from trusted sources and review code before importing. A malicious Function could access your file system, exfiltrate data, or compromise your entire system.

Browse the [Community Function Library](https://openwebui.com/search) . Click **Get** on the function you want. Enter your Open WebUI instance URL (e.g., `http://localhost:3000` ). Click **Import to Open WebUI** . You'll be redirected to the Function Editor. Review the code, then click **Save** . warning Always review the source code before importing. Community functions are user-contributed and **run directly on your server** .
A Pipe registers itself as a new "model" in Open WebUI. When a user selects it and sends a message, the `pipe()` method handles the entire request with no LLM backend required.

A Filter sits between the user and the model, intercepting data at three stages: **`inlet()`** : Modifies the request **before** it reaches the model (add context, sanitize input, detect language, enforce rate limits, estimate token costs). **`stream()`** : Intercepts **streamed chunks** from the model in real time (censor content, replace terms, track token usage). **`outlet()`** : Processes the completed response **after** it's generated (log to observability platforms, format citations, append disclaimers, cache responses).
Filters can be applied globally (to all models) or attached to specific models. Toggleable filters let users enable/disable them per-chat.

Toggleable Filters ​ Filters can be made user-toggleable by setting `self.toggle = True` in `__init__` . When toggleable, users see an on/off switch in the chat input area and can enable or disable the filter per-conversation. Filters without `self.toggle` are always-on when active.

An Action adds a custom button to the chat message toolbar. When a user clicks it, the `action()` method runs with full access to the event system for real-time UI feedback, user prompts, and confirmations.

An Event function runs custom Python in response to **system events** (a user signs up, a chat is deleted, the server starts, configuration changes). Its `event()` method is called for every event and filters on the event name. Event functions can register their own API endpoints and call internal services, which suits them to lifecycle automation, audit logging, signup gating, provisioning, and self-installing plugins.

Functions support a two-tier configuration system built on [Pydantic](https://docs.pydantic.dev/) : |Level |Class Name |Who Configures |Where | |**Admin** |`Valves` |Administrators only |Admin Panel → Functions → ⚙️ | |**User** |`UserValves` |Any user |Chat interface, per-function | **Valves** are ideal for API keys, model endpoints, and global behavior settings. **UserValves** let individual users customize behavior (e.g., their preferred language, output format, or personal API key). Both are defined as nested Pydantic `BaseModel` classes inside your `Pipe` , `Filter` , or `Action` class. The admin-configured values are stored in the database and loaded automatically at runtime.

Open WebUI supports four types of Functions. The type is **auto-detected** from the class name in your Python code, so you never need to configure it manually. |Type |Class Name |What It Does |How Users See It | |**Pipe** |`class Pipe` |Adds a custom model or agent |Appears as a selectable model in the chat sidebar | |**Filter** |`class Filter` |Intercepts data flowing to/from models |Runs transparently as middleware on existing models | |**Action** |`class Action` |Adds interactive buttons to messages |Appears as a clickable button on chat messages | |**Event** |`class Event` |Runs custom logic in response to system events |Runs in the background; no direct UI | Pipe Functions ​ A Pipe registers itself as a new "model" in Open WebUI. When a user selects it and sends a message, the `pipe()` method handles the entire request with no LLM backend required. This makes Pipes incredibly versatile: **Model providers** : Integrate APIs that don't follow the OpenAI protocol (Anthropic native, Google Vertex, custom inference servers). **Agents & workflows** : Build multi-step agents that call tools, search the web, and reason across multiple turns. **Non-LLM interfaces** : Create a smart home controller, a database query tool, a search engine, a calculator, or a code executor. Anything that takes user input and returns a response. **Proxies & routers** : Route requests through your own logic, add caching, load balancing, or cost tracking. A single Pipe can also expose **multiple models** (called a "manifold") by defining a `pipes()` method that returns a list of model identifiers. → **Pipe Function Guide** Filter Functions ​ A Filter sits between the user and the model, intercepting data at three stages: **`inlet()`** : Modifies the request **before** it reaches the model (add context, sanitize input, detect language, enforce rate limits, estimate token costs). **`stream()`** : Intercepts **streamed chunks** from the model in real time (censor content, replace terms, track token usage). **`outlet()`** : Processes the completed response **after** it's generated (log to observability platforms, format citations, append disclaimers, cache responses). Filters enable powerful cross-cutting concerns like real-time translation, content moderation, prompt injection detection, A/B testing, compliance logging, and PII redaction, all without modifying the underlying model. Filters can be applied globally (to all models) or attached to specific models. Toggleable filters let users enable/disable them per-chat. → **Filter Function Guide** Action Functions ​ An Action adds a custom button to the chat message toolbar. When a user clicks it, the `action()` method runs with full access to the event system for real-time UI feedback, user prompts, and confirmations. Actions can do anything Python can do: summarize or translate a message, copy formatted output, pin important messages, export conversations to external systems, trigger a CI/CD pipeline, send a Slack notification, generate a PDF report, run a code snippet, or kick off an external workflow. → **Action Function Guide** Event Functions ​ _New in Open WebUI 0.10.0._ An Event function runs custom Python in response to **system events** (a user signs up, a chat is deleted, the server starts, configuration changes). Its `event()` method is called for every event and filters on the event name. Event functions can register their own API endpoints and call internal services, which suits them to lifecycle automation, audit logging, signup gating, provisioning, and self-installing plugins.

Functions are **modular Python plugins** that extend the capabilities of Open WebUI itself. While Tools give LLMs the ability to call external APIs during inference, Functions change how the platform behaves at a deeper level. They can add entirely new "models" powered by any Python logic, intercept and transform every message flowing through the system, or place interactive buttons directly in the chat UI. The possibilities are broad: connect a proprietary AI provider, build a smart home controller that responds to natural language, create a database query interface, add real-time translation to every conversation, enforce compliance policies, generate charts from data, or trigger external workflows with a button click. If you can write it in Python, you can turn it into a Function. Functions are stored in the database as Python source code, dynamically loaded at runtime, and executed server-side. Administrators create and manage them; regular users interact with the results.

excerpts: MCP Support / Open WebUI This documentation explains how to easily set up and deploy the MCP (Model Context Protocol)-to-OpenAPI proxy server (mcpo) provided by Open WebUI.
Learn how you can expose MCP-based tool servers using standard, familiar OpenAPI endpoints suitable for end-users and developers.

This documentation explains how to easily set up and deploy the [**MCP (Model Context Protocol)-to-OpenAPI proxy server** (mcpo)](https://github.com/open-webui/mcpo) provided by Open WebUI. Learn how you can expose MCP-based tool servers using standard, familiar OpenAPI endpoints suitable for end-users and developers.
This page covers `mcpo` , the MCP-to-OpenAPI bridge.

The MCP-to-OpenAPI proxy server lets you use tool servers implemented with MCP (Model Context Protocol) directly via standard REST/OpenAPI APIs, with no need to manage unfamiliar or complicated custom protocols. If you're an end-user or application developer, this means you can interact easily with powerful MCP-based tooling directly through familiar REST-like endpoints.

While MCP tool servers are powerful and flexible, they commonly communicate via standard input/output (stdio), often running on your local machine where they can easily access your filesystem, environment, and other native system capabilities. That’s a strength, but also a limitation. If you want to deploy your main interface (like Open WebUI) on the cloud, you quickly run into a problem: your cloud instance can’t speak directly to an MCP server running locally on your machine via stdio.

MCP servers typically rely on raw stdio communication, which is: 🔓 Inherently insecure across environments ❌ Incompatible with most modern tools, UIs, or platforms 🧩 Lacking critical features like authentication, documentation, and error handling

The mcpo proxy addresses those issues: ✅ Instantly compatible with existing OpenAPI tools, SDKs, and clients 🛡 Wraps your tools with secure, scalable, and standards-based HTTP endpoints 🧠 Auto-generates interactive OpenAPI documentation for every tool, entirely config-free 🔌 Uses plain HTTP, with no socket setup, daemon juggling, or platform-specific glue code

**Prerequisites** **Python 3.8+** with `pip` installed. MCP-compatible application (for example: `mcp-server-time` ) (Optional but recommended) `uv` installed for faster startup and zero-config convenience.
**Install mcpo** Using **uv** (recommended): ``` uvx mcpo --port 8000 -- your_mcp_server_command ```

🔑 **Translating this MCP setup to a quick local proxy command** : You can easily run the recommended MCP server ( `mcp-server-time` ) directly through the **MCP-to-OpenAPI proxy** ( `mcpo` ) like this: ``` uvx mcpo --port 8000 -- uvx mcp-server-time --local-timezone=America/New_York ``` That's it! You're now running the MCP-to-OpenAPI Proxy locally and exposing the powerful **MCP Time Server** through standard OpenAPI endpoints accessible at: 📖 **Interactive OpenAPI Documentation:** [`http://localhost:8000/docs`](http://localhost:8000/docs) Feel free to replace `uvx mcp-server-time --local-timezone=America/New_York` with your preferred MCP Server command from other available MCP implementations found in the official repository.

🚀 Accessing the Generated APIs ​ As soon as it starts, the MCP Proxy ( `mcpo` ) automatically: Discovers MCP tools dynamically and generates REST endpoints. Creates interactive, human-readable OpenAPI documentation accessible at: `http://localhost:8000/docs` Simply call the auto-generated API endpoints directly via HTTP clients, AI agents, or other OpenAPI tools of your preference.

**Dynamic Schema Discovery & Endpoints:** At server startup, the proxy connects to the MCP server to query available tools. It automatically builds FastAPI endpoints based on the MCP tool schemas, creating concise and clear REST endpoints. **OpenAPI Auto-documentation:** Endpoints generated are seamlessly documented and available via FastAPI's built-in Swagger UI ( `/docs` ). No extra doc writing required.

If you want to use the published mcpo image instead of building your own image, bind the proxy to `0.0.0.0` so Docker port publishing can reach it: ``` docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/open-webui/mcpo:main \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ --api-key "top-secret" \ -- your_mcp_server_command ```

Critical for Persistence If you connect Open WebUI to this proxy using an API Key or Auth Token, you **MUST** set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` in your Open WebUI Docker config. If this key changes (e.g., on container restart), Open WebUI will fail to decrypt the stored credentials for your tool.

``` docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/open-webui/mcpo:main \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ --api-key "top-secret" \ -- your_mcp_server_command ```

**Dockerfile Example** Create the following `Dockerfile` inside your deployment directory: ``` FROM python:3.11-slim WORKDIR /app RUN pip install mcpo uv # Replace with your MCP server command; example: uvx mcp-server-time CMD [ "uvx" , "mcpo" , "--host" , "0.0.0.0" , "--port" , "8000" , "--" , "uvx" , "mcp-server-time" , "--local-timezone=America/New_York" ] ``` **Build & Run the Container Locally** ``` docker build -t mcp-proxy-server . docker run -d -p 8000:8000 mcp-proxy-server ``` If you want to use the published mcpo image instead of building your own image, bind the proxy to `0.0.0.0` so Docker port publishing can reach it: ``` docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/open-webui/mcpo:main \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ --api-key "top-secret" \ -- your_mcp_server_command ``` For Docker Compose, put the same mcpo arguments in the service command: ``` services : mcpo : image : ghcr.io/open-webui/mcpo:main ports : - "8000:8000" command : - --host - 0.0.0.0 - --port - "8000" - --api-key - top-secret - -- - your_mcp_server_command ``` Replace `your_mcp_server_command` with your MCP server command, adding each argument as its own `command` list item. excerpts: Quick Start / Open WebUI docker-run.sh: Builds the Open WebUI image and runs a single container, exposing it on OPEN_WEBUI_PORT (default 3000). docker-ollama.sh: Pulls and runs the official Ollama container with optional GPU passthrough, exposing it on OLLAMA_PORT (default 11434).
**Docker:** Officially supported and recommended for most users. Requires [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) installed.
1\. Pull the image ​ ``` docker pull ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main ```
2\. Run the container ​ ``` docker run -d -p 3000:8080 -v open-webui:/app/backend/data --name open-webui ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main ```
|Flag |Purpose | |`-v open-webui:/app/backend/data` |Persistent storage. Prevents data loss between restarts. | |`-p 3000:8080` |Exposes the UI on port 3000 of your machine. |
3\. Open the UI ​ Visit <http://localhost:3000> .

Docker Hub Now Available Open WebUI images are published to **both** registries: **GitHub Container Registry:** `ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui` **Docker Hub:** `openwebui/open-webui` Both contain identical images.

`:main` and `:latest` are the **same rolling image** : both point to the newest build from the `main` branch and are rebuilt every time a change lands there, so their digest moves forward as development continues. Note that `:latest` follows `main` ; it does **not** point to the newest stable release. `:dev` is the same idea for the `dev` branch (upcoming features), also rolling. Version tags, such as `:vX.Y.Z` and the shorter `:X.Y.Z` and `:X.Y` , are **pinned** to one stable release and never change. `:git-<commit-sha>` pins one exact commit. This is why `:main` and a specific release tag can show different image digests at the same time: `:main` already includes everything merged since that release, while the version tag stays frozen at it. |Tag |Points to |Immutable? | |`:main` , `:latest` |Newest build of the `main` branch |No (rolling) | |`:dev` |Newest build of the `dev` branch |No (rolling) | |`:vX.Y.Z` , `:X.Y.Z` , `:X.Y` |A specific stable release |Yes | |`:git-<sha>` |One exact commit |Yes | For reproducible or production deployments, pin a version tag.

Specific release versions ​ For production environments, pin a specific version instead of using floating tags. excerpts: Open WebUI's **stateless, container-first architecture** means the same application runs identically whether you deploy it as a Python process on a VM, a container in a managed service, or a pod in a Kubernetes cluster.
The difference between deployment patterns is how you **orchestrate, scale, and operate** the application, not how the application itself behaves.
Open WebUI supports three production deployment patterns.
Run the official Open WebUI container image on a managed platform such as AWS ECS/Fargate, Azure Container Apps, or Google Cloud Run.
Best for teams wanting container benefits (immutable images, versioned deployments, no OS management) without Kubernetes complexity.

|**Container isolation** |None (process runs directly on OS) |Full container isolation |Full container + namespace isolation | |**Rolling updates** |Manual (scale down, update, scale up) |Platform-managed rolling deployments |Declarative rolling updates with rollback |
Regardless of which deployment pattern you choose, every scaled Open WebUI deployment requires the same set of backing services.
Configure these **before** scaling beyond a single instance.

|**PostgreSQL** |Multi-instance deployments require a real database. SQLite does not support concurrent writes from multiple processes. |Self-managed, Amazon RDS, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Google Cloud SQL |
|**Redis** |Session management, WebSocket coordination, and configuration sync across instances. |Self-managed, Amazon ElastiCache, Azure Cache for Redis, Google Memorystore |
|**Shared Storage** |Uploaded files must be accessible from every instance. |Shared filesystem (NFS, EFS, CephFS) or object storage ( `S3` , `GCS` , `Azure Blob` ) |
These environment variables **must** be set consistently across every instance:

Shared secret — MUST be identical on all instances WEBUI_SECRET_KEY = your-secret-key-here # Database DATABASE_URL = postgresql://user:password@db-host:5432/openwebui # Vector Database VECTOR_DB = pgvector PGVECTOR_DB_URL = postgresql://user:password@db-host:5432/openwebui # Redis REDIS_URL = redis://redis-host:6379/0 WEBSOCKET_MANAGER = redis ENABLE_WEBSOCKET_SUPPORT = true # Content Extraction CONTENT_EXTRACTION_ENGINE = tika TIKA_SERVER_URL = http://tika:9998 # Embeddings RAG_EMBEDDING_ENGINE = openai # Storage — choose ONE: # Option A: shared filesystem (mount the same volume to all instances, no env var needed) # Option B: object storage (see https://docs.openwebui.com/reference/env-configuration for all required vars) # STORAGE_PROVIDER=s3 # Workers — let the orchestrator handle scaling UVICORN_WORKERS = 1 # Migrations — only ONE instance should run migrations ENABLE_DB_MIGRATIONS = false
Set `ENABLE_DB_MIGRATIONS=false` on **all instances except one** .
During updates, scale down to a single instance, allow migrations to complete, then scale back up.
Concurrent migrations can corrupt your database.
**`/health`** : Basic liveness check. Returns HTTP 200 when the application is running. Use this for load balancer and auto-scaler health checks.

Set `ENABLE_DB_MIGRATIONS=false` on **all instances except one** . During updates, scale down to a single instance, allow migrations to complete, then scale back up. Concurrent migrations can corrupt your database.

Python / Pip on Auto-Scaling VMs ​ Deploy `open-webui serve` as a systemd-managed process on virtual machines in a cloud auto-scaling group (AWS ASG, Azure VMSS, GCP MIG). Best for teams with established VM-based infrastructure and strong Linux administration skills, or when regulatory requirements mandate direct OS-level control. Container Service ​ Run the official Open WebUI container image on a managed platform such as AWS ECS/Fargate, Azure Container Apps, or Google Cloud Run. Best for teams wanting container benefits (immutable images, versioned deployments, no OS management) without Kubernetes complexity. Kubernetes with Helm ​ Deploy using the official Open WebUI Helm chart on any Kubernetes distribution (EKS, AKS, GKE, OpenShift, Rancher, self-managed). Best for large-scale, mission-critical deployments requiring declarative infrastructure-as-code, advanced auto-scaling, and GitOps workflows.

content.executive_summary:
- **Layered Runtime**: The current repository separates a SvelteKit client from a Python backend, with FastAPI routers, REST, Socket.IO, static serving, and health endpoints -> keep UI, policy, provider, and persistence concerns as separate fork modules. [executive_summary[0]] [25] [executive_summary[1]] [31]
- **Protocol-First Providers**: Open WebUI targets OpenAI-compatible APIs rather than a bespoke adapter for every vendor, while still supporting Ollama and local servers -> make a Kolb-Bot-style fork provider-neutral and put vendor-specific behavior behind a compatible gateway or Pipe. [executive_summary[2]] [17] [executive_summary[2]] [17]
- **Configurable Knowledge**: Knowledge supports focused RAG retrieval, full-context injection, hybrid BM25 plus vector search, and model-attached collections -> tune chunking, embeddings, access scope, and context length instead of hard-coding one retrieval strategy. [executive_summary[3]] [13] [executive_summary[3]] [13] [executive_summary[4]] [15]
- **Self-Hosted Identity**: OAuth/OIDC, trusted headers, encrypted server-side OAuth sessions, and role mapping cover both standalone and enterprise-style deployments -> treat redirect URLs, role claims, proxy trust, and secret management as first-class fork configuration. [executive_summary[5]] [20] [executive_summary[5]] [20]
- **Two Extension Planes**: Tools give models callable capabilities; Functions change platform behavior through server-side Python, including Pipes, Filters, Actions, and Events -> use Tools or MCP for integrations and reserve Functions for controlled platform policy or UI behavior. [executive_summary[6]] [28] [executive_summary[7]] [23]
- **Docker Simplicity, Scale-Out Discipline**: The one-container quick start persists `/app/backend/data`, while multi-instance operation requires PostgreSQL, Redis, shared files, and a multi-process-safe vector backend -> do not confuse a stateless app process with stateless application data. [executive_summary[8]] [24] [executive_summary[9]] [6]
- **MCP Interoperability**: Native HTTP MCP and the mcpo bridge make remote and local MCP servers usable as OpenAPI-style tools -> standardize tool ingress, authentication, and network boundaries rather than embedding every integration in the fork. [executive_summary[10]] [29] [executive_summary[11]] [22]
- **Security Boundary**: Workspace Tools and Functions execute arbitrary Python on the server, and trusted-header role injection can grant admin access -> install only reviewed code, restrict permissions, isolate risky workers where possible, and never treat community plugins as harmless UI add-ons. [executive_summary[7]] [23] [executive_summary[10]] [29] [executive_summary[5]] [20]

The public sources are sufficient for the Open WebUI architecture and fork strategy. They do not establish a separate, authoritative implementation layout for Kolb-Bot itself, so the Kolb-Bot recommendations below are design guidance rather than claims about that fork's private or undocumented code.
content.1_repository_shape_and_request_boundary:
The repository is a monorepo-style application with visible top-level `backend/`, `src/`, `static/`, `docs/`, and `scripts/` directories, plus `Dockerfile`, `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, and `vite.config.ts`. That layout is important for a fork: the web client, Python service, build metadata, and image recipe are versioned together rather than maintained as unrelated products. [1_repository_shape_and_request_boundary[0]] [1]

The frontend is a SvelteKit single-page application with hierarchical routing and Svelte-store state management. It communicates with the backend through REST APIs and Socket.IO, which gives the UI a conventional request path for CRUD/configuration work and a realtime path for streaming or event-oriented behavior. [1_repository_shape_and_request_boundary[1]] [25] The current package manifest identifies Svelte 5.53.10, SvelteKit 2.5.27, Vite 5.4.21, TypeScript 5.5.4, Tailwind CSS 4.0.0, and Node support from 18.13 through the 22.x line. [1_repository_shape_and_request_boundary[2]] [27]

The backend creates a FastAPI application and uses an asynchronous lifespan for startup and shutdown. Startup initializes configuration, migrations and defaults, optional admin creation, Redis and tool or terminal services, and readiness state. Middleware includes authentication-token handling, session commit, security headers, compression, CORS, and a WebSocket-upgrade guard. [1_repository_shape_and_request_boundary[3]] [31] [1_repository_shape_and_request_boundary[3]] [31]

At runtime, the backend mounts the realtime Socket.IO application at `/ws`, registers Ollama and OpenAI routes plus application routers for pipelines, tasks, images, audio, retrieval, configuration, authentication, and related functions, and serves the compiled frontend as an SPA at `/`. It exposes `/health` for liveness and `/ready` for readiness checks that include startup, database, and configured Redis status. [1_repository_shape_and_request_boundary[3]] [31]

| Layer | Current implementation | Best fork boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Browser UI | SvelteKit SPA, Svelte stores, REST, Socket.IO | `src/`, static assets, routes, components, stores |
| Application service | FastAPI with async lifespan and middleware | `backend/open_webui/`, routers, services, policies |
| Model boundary | Ollama and OpenAI-compatible routes and connections | Provider configuration, gateway, Pipe, or new adapter |
| Data and retrieval | SQLAlchemy/Alembic, files, embeddings, vector backends | Database/storage configuration and retrieval modules |
| Build and release | `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, Dockerfile and Compose | Brand, image, build args, pinned release workflow |

The practical architectural pattern is therefore browser -> authenticated FastAPI boundary -> provider, retrieval, storage, and tool services. The exact sequence varies by feature, but the separation is clear enough to support a branded fork without rewriting the model runtime.
content.2_backend_and_data_plane_technology_stac:
The Python project requires Python 3.11 or 3.12 and uses FastAPI 0.136.3, Uvicorn 0.51.0, and Pydantic 2.13.4. Its persistence layer includes SQLAlchemy's async support, SQLite through aiosqlite, PostgreSQL through psycopg, and Alembic migrations. [2_backend_and_data_plane_technology_stack[0]] [9] [2_backend_and_data_plane_technology_stack[0]] [9] This is a pragmatic choice for a self-hosted product: SQLite lowers the barrier for a personal installation, while PostgreSQL provides the concurrency model needed for shared deployments.

The security and identity stack includes `cryptography`, `bcrypt`, `argon2-cffi`, `PyJWT`, Authlib, and JOSE support, while `python-socketio` supplies the Python side of realtime communication. HTTP and network integration uses `requests`, `aiohttp`, and `httpx` with HTTP/2, compression, and proxy-related extras. [2_backend_and_data_plane_technology_stack[0]] [9] The dependency set also includes document parsers, Transformers, Sentence Transformers, ChromaDB, OpenSearch, and multiple optional vector/database clients. [2_backend_and_data_plane_technology_stack[0]] [9] [2_backend_and_data_plane_technology_stack[0]] [9]

The backend source makes a meaningful operational distinction between app code and backing services. A single process can use local SQLite, local files, and a local vector store. A scaled deployment cannot simply multiply that process and expect correctness: SQLite does not support concurrent multi-process writes, Redis is needed for sessions, WebSocket coordination, and configuration synchronization, and uploaded files must be reachable by every instance. [2_backend_and_data_plane_technology_stack[1]] [6]

For a Kolb-Bot-style fork, the useful design is to keep the backend's stable contracts intact and add a domain layer around them. A domain-specific prompt policy, retrieval namespace, or model catalog can be implemented as configuration, a Filter, a Pipe, or a separate service before changing core routers. A core code change is justified when the fork needs a new authorization invariant, persistence model, or UI workflow that cannot be expressed through those boundaries.

One licensing point deserves attention before publishing a fork. The repository metadata says that the project contains code under multiple licenses, including the Open WebUI License with an additional requirement to preserve the Open WebUI branding, alongside earlier contributions under their original licenses. A fork should review the repository's current license files and preserve required notices before replacing the product name or redistributing an image. [2_backend_and_data_plane_technology_stack[2]] [1]
content.3_core_product_capabilities:
| Capability | How it works | Fork implication | Main caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chat and models | SvelteKit UI calls FastAPI model routes; providers can expose local or cloud models | Add model policy and defaults without coupling the UI to one vendor | Provider-specific behavior belongs behind a protocol or Pipe |
| Knowledge | Files and collections are attached to models or referenced with `#` | Create domain knowledge packs and access scopes | Processing and embedding are asynchronous |
| RAG | Query embedding, vector retrieval, chunking, optional hybrid search and reranking | Tune per corpus and re-index after embedding changes | Context size and embedding compatibility determine quality |
| Identity | OAuth/OIDC, trusted headers, sessions, role mapping | Integrate an existing identity perimeter | A trusted role header can become an admin escalation path |
| Tools and MCP | Python Tools, OpenAPI endpoints, native HTTP MCP, or mcpo for stdio MCP | Keep integrations outside core code where possible | Tool and Function code runs with server-side authority |

### Chat and model connectivity

Open WebUI's model boundary is deliberately protocol-oriented. It connects to any provider implementing an OpenAI-compatible API and can use a Pipe or middleware such as LiteLLM or OpenRouter when a provider does not fit that protocol. The setup is URL plus API key, and providers without a `/models` endpoint can still work when model IDs are manually supplied. [3_core_product_capabilities[0]] [17] The documented examples span cloud vendors, gateways, Llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM, LocalAI, and other local or remote servers. [3_core_product_capabilities[0]] [17] [3_core_product_capabilities[0]] [17]

That choice is more than convenience. It makes the UI a control plane for multiple inference backends and lets a fork define a stable model catalog while changing the actual inference server behind it. For Kolb-Bot, a good default is to expose organization-approved models through one or more compatible endpoints and let the fork's policy layer control visibility, defaults, system prompts, and tool access.

### Knowledge and RAG

A Knowledge base stores files and collections such as PDFs, spreadsheets, code, and text documents. Focused Retrieval uses RAG to find and inject relevant chunks, while Full Context inserts the complete file without chunking or semantic search. Knowledge can be attached to a model or referenced in chat, and access may be scoped to attached collections or broadened to everything the user can access. [3_core_product_capabilities[1]] [13] [3_core_product_capabilities[1]] [13] [3_core_product_capabilities[1]] [13] [3_core_product_capabilities[1]] [13]

The RAG path is tunable: chunk size and overlap affect context continuity, small Markdown sections may be merged, and query embeddings are compared against the vector database before top matches enter the prompt. Hybrid search can combine BM25 keyword search, vector search, and reranking. [3_core_product_capabilities[2]] [15] [3_core_product_capabilities[2]] [15] [3_core_product_capabilities[1]] [13] The stored vectors must match the configured embedding model and dimensions, and changing the embedding model requires re-indexing the corpus. [3_core_product_capabilities[2]] [15] [3_core_product_capabilities[2]] [15]

Native function calling changes the data path: attached Knowledge is not necessarily injected automatically; the model may need to call Knowledge tools such as semantic retrieval, exact-match search, or filesystem-style browsing. [3_core_product_capabilities[1]] [13] [3_core_product_capabilities[1]] [13] That is useful for agentic forks, but it makes tool permissions, model tool behavior, and retrieval observability part of the product design.

### OAuth and SSO

The SSO implementation supports OAuth, OIDC, and trusted-header patterns. `ENABLE_OAUTH` enables provider sign-in, `ENABLE_OAUTH_SIGNUP` controls account creation at OAuth login, and `WEBUI_URL` supplies the redirect base. The documented configuration includes Google, Microsoft, and arbitrary OIDC providers, with provider-specific callback paths and a required email claim for generic OIDC. [3_core_product_capabilities[3]] [20] [3_core_product_capabilities[3]] [20] [3_core_product_capabilities[3]] [20]

Open WebUI supports provider role mapping through `OAUTH_ROLES_CLAIM`, allowed-role and admin-role settings, and an enable switch. Trusted headers can provide email, groups, and roles through a reverse proxy, but the documentation warns that an untrusted client must never be able to set a role header. OAuth tokens are encrypted and stored server-side while the browser receives an opaque session identifier; refresh tokens support renewal and multiple sessions are supported. [3_core_product_capabilities[3]] [20] [3_core_product_capabilities[3]] [20]
content.4_docker_and_deployment_patterns:
The simplest supported pattern is one Open WebUI container with a named data volume:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
docker run -d -p 3000:8080 -v open-webui:/app/backend/data --name open-webui ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
```

The volume preserves application data across container replacement, and the UI is exposed on host port 3000. The documentation recommends immutable version tags for production rather than rolling `main` or `latest` tags. [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[0]] [24] [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[0]] [24]

The repository Compose pattern adds an Ollama service. Ollama uses its own named volume at `/root/.ollama`; Open WebUI uses `open-webui:/app/backend/data`, depends on Ollama, maps `${OPEN_WEBUI_PORT-3000}:8080`, and points to `http://ollama:11434` over the Compose network. The WebUI service also sets `host.docker.internal:host-gateway`, which supports connections to a host-side service when needed. [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[1]] [26]

The Dockerfile is a build-time customization point. It builds the frontend with Node 22 Alpine, runs the Python service on Python 3.11 slim, and exposes build arguments for CUDA, bundled Ollama, slim images, permission hardening, and UID/GID selection. It includes a health check at `/health`, defaults the RAG embedding model to `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, and runs the final container as the configured UID/GID. [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[2]] [32] [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[2]] [32] [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[2]] [32]

| Deployment mode | Appropriate use | Required design discipline |
|---|---|---|
| Single Docker container | Personal or small team installation | Persist `/app/backend/data`; pin the image tag |
| Compose with Ollama | Local all-in-one inference stack | Use the service DNS name and persist both named volumes |
| Managed container or VM | Controlled production service | Use `/health`, externalize state, and manage secrets |
| Multiple WebUI replicas | Higher availability or load | PostgreSQL, Redis, shared file storage, and safe vector backend |
| Kubernetes | Organization-wide operation | Use shared backing services and the documented health/readiness model |

The scale-out rule is explicit: PostgreSQL replaces SQLite for concurrent writes, Redis coordinates sessions and WebSockets, uploaded files need shared storage such as NFS, EFS, CephFS, or object storage, and local ChromaDB SQLite mode must be replaced by a multi-process-safe backend or HTTP mode. [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[3]] [6] The `/health` endpoint is intended for load balancers and auto-scalers. [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[3]] [6]

### Case study: the official Compose boundary

Open WebUI's own Compose file is a compact case study in separation of concerns. It places Ollama and the UI in distinct services, gives each its own persistence volume, and connects them through the internal service name rather than baking an inference engine into the UI process. [4_docker_and_deployment_patterns[1]] [26] The outcome is a local stack that is easy to start while preserving the same provider boundary used for remote APIs.

That decision reveals the right fork strategy: bundle a convenient development inference path, but do not make the product depend on it. A Kolb-Bot-style fork can ship a local Compose profile for onboarding and a production profile that points to an external gateway or managed model service. The UI and policy code remain unchanged while deployment changes around them.
content.5_extension_and_fork_customization_point:
Open WebUI offers a ladder of customization from lowest risk to deepest control:

1. **Environment configuration**: Change API headers, CORS, model access, retrieval access, Chroma connection, chunking, overlap, and provider keys without changing source. For example, `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN` controls allowed origins, `CHROMA_HTTP_HOST` enables remote Chroma, and `CHUNK_SIZE` and `CHUNK_OVERLAP` tune ingestion. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[0]] [12] [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[0]] [12] [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[0]] [12]
2. **Provider and model configuration**: Add OpenAI-compatible connections, model allowlists, gateways, or a Pipe. This is the preferred place for a domain-specific model catalog. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[1]] [17] [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[1]] [17]
3. **Workspace Tools**: Add Python tools that models can call, import OpenAPI JSON or YAML so every endpoint becomes a tool, connect directly to HTTP/SSE MCP, or use mcpo for local stdio servers. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[2]] [29]
4. **Functions**: Add server-side platform behavior. Pipe Functions register new models; Filters transform inbound requests or streamed and completed output; Actions add chat-toolbar buttons; Event Functions react to system events. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[3]] [23]
5. **External tool services**: Use mcpo to discover MCP schemas and expose FastAPI REST endpoints documented through Swagger, with API-key or other standard authentication. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[4]] [22] [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[4]] [22]
6. **Source fork**: When configuration and extensions are insufficient, modify the SvelteKit source, backend routers/services, package and Python manifests, static assets, and Docker build. Keep the patch narrow and rebaseable.

Tools and Functions should not be conflated. Tools extend what the model can do and are managed in the Workspace, while Functions extend how the platform behaves and are managed by administrators. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[5]] [28] [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[5]] [28] Functions are stored as Python source in the database, dynamically loaded, and executed server-side. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[3]] [23]

The security consequence is substantial. Workspace Tools and Functions execute arbitrary Python on the server, and the documentation restricts creation or management to trusted users. Function code can access the filesystem or exfiltrate data, so a fork should review code before import, avoid hard-coded API keys, use Valves or equivalent configuration, and consider a separate worker or process boundary for untrusted integrations. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[3]] [23] [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[6]] [33] [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[2]] [29]

Pipelines are a migration concern. The documentation calls them legacy and maps the old pipe and filter patterns to in-process Pipe and Filter Functions, which avoid a separate worker container for those cases. [5_extension_and_fork_customization_points[7]] [21] A fork starting today should use current Functions for local behavior and reserve a separate Pipelines-style service for integrations that truly need process isolation or an independent deployment lifecycle.
content.6_design_decisions_for_a_kolb_bot_style_:
| Decision | Benefit | Trade-off | Recommended fork treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenAI-compatible protocol boundary | Many local and cloud providers work through one integration path | Lowest-common-denominator API behavior | Keep model policy separate from transport; add middleware for special APIs |
| SPA plus FastAPI service | Clear UI/service ownership and simple container packaging | Changes can cross TypeScript and Python boundaries | Define a small API contract and add tests around it |
| Built-in RAG and Knowledge | Fast path from uploaded files to searchable context | Embedding, chunk, and context settings can silently degrade quality | Version embedding settings and re-index deliberately |
| In-process Python extensions | Very powerful, low-friction customization | Extension code has server authority | Allowlist, review, audit, and isolate risky code |
| Persistent local mode plus scale-out services | Easy personal deployment and a credible production path | Two operational profiles must be supported | Ship Compose for development and external PostgreSQL/Redis/storage for scale |
| Configurable identity and access control | Fits standalone, OAuth, OIDC, and proxy-managed environments | Misconfigured role headers or access bypasses are dangerous | Make secure defaults and deployment checks part of the fork |

For a fork, the most maintainable architecture is a thin product layer over Open WebUI rather than a permanent divergence of every core screen and router. Put branding, navigation defaults, model visibility, system prompts, Knowledge presets, and domain tools in configuration or extension surfaces first. Put only durable domain invariants, such as a new data model or mandatory authorization rule, in the backend source.

Use the protocol boundary for inference and the MCP/OpenAPI boundary for integrations. A domain tool should ideally be independently testable and deployable, with the fork attaching it through Workspace Tools, HTTP MCP, or mcpo. This reduces the blast radius of provider changes and makes the same tool available to a future non-Open-WebUI client.

Treat Knowledge as a product subsystem rather than a file-upload checkbox. Define corpus ownership, retrieval scope, embedding model, chunk policy, re-index procedure, and observability. If native function calling is enabled, test both automatic retrieval and explicit Knowledge-tool calls because they are different runtime paths. [6_design_decisions_for_a_kolb_bot_style_fork[0]] [13]

Finally, make the deployment profile explicit. A local Kolb-Bot image can use the named data volume and bundled Ollama pattern. A production image should pin releases, set a durable `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY`, use external PostgreSQL and Redis, use shared file storage, and put MCP or plugin services behind an authenticated network boundary. Changing the secret key can prevent stored tool credentials from being decrypted, so secret rotation needs a migration plan rather than an ad hoc environment edit. content.synthesis:
Open WebUI combines three strategies that are often separated in self-hosted AI products. First, it is a protocol-oriented model client: the OpenAI-compatible boundary favors breadth and replaceability over vendor-specific depth. Second, it is a data application: Knowledge, RAG, identity, files, and sessions require durable state and explicit access control. Third, it is a programmable platform: Tools, Functions, MCP, and source-level hooks let administrators alter model capabilities and application behavior.

The strategies differ in scope and risk. Provider configuration is broad but comparatively low risk; it changes where inference runs without changing core behavior. Knowledge configuration is medium risk because chunking, embeddings, and context limits affect answer quality while remaining bounded to retrieval. Functions and Tools are high power and high risk because arbitrary Python runs with server authority. MCP is a useful middle layer when tools should be remote, separately deployed, or shared across clients. [synthesis[0]] [17] [synthesis[1]] [13] [synthesis[2]] [23] [synthesis[3]] [22]

The main tension is between simplicity and scale. The one-container Docker pattern makes local deployment approachable, but multi-instance operation needs PostgreSQL, Redis, shared files, and a safe vector architecture. The app can be treated as a stateless replica only after its stateful dependencies are externalized. [synthesis[4]] [24] [synthesis[5]] [6]

The second tension is between extensibility and supply-chain security. In-process plugins are more convenient than a separate service, but they collapse the boundary between extension and host. A fork that values long-term maintainability should use configuration and protocol integrations for ordinary features, reserve Functions for reviewed trusted code, and isolate integrations that need stronger containment.

The resulting recommendation is a layered fork: retain Open WebUI's SvelteKit/FastAPI core and provider protocol; add domain policy through configuration and narrow Functions; expose reusable integrations through OpenAPI or MCP; externalize persistence before scaling; and keep branding and source changes small enough to rebase. That gives a Kolb-Bot-style product a distinct experience without sacrificing the upstream platform's deployment and provider flexibility.
